analysis.one_liner: Bars new federal oil and gas leases to companies that don't develop or give up the leases they already hold.
analysis.headline: The House passed it with 223 votes, but that fell short of the two-thirds required, so the bill died.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2008 gas-price spike, this bill said that oil and gas companies holding federal leases where they were not drilling would have to either start producing or give the leases back, before they could get any new federal leases. It also shortened lease terms, required a development plan from every leaseholder, imposed fines for noncompliance, and doubled the rent for renewing a lease that had not reached production. The bill got a yes-or-no vote in the House under a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority to pass. It received 223 votes to 195, short of the roughly 290 needed, and never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and energy consumers, by pushing companies to drill on federal land they already hold instead of stockpiling unused leases — more domestic supply at a moment of record gasoline prices — plus taxpayers who would collect doubled rents and penalties rather than see public acreage sit idle.

how_it_helps.text: It barred the Interior Department from issuing any new oil or gas lease to a company that was not diligently developing, or willing to relinquish, its existing federal leases.
It required regulations with benchmarks ensuring production within the five-year original lease term, a development plan from each leaseholder, and civil penalties for noncompliance.

It rewrote lease terms so leases run five years with one-year renewals only if production is occurring or genuinely progressing, and renewal rents double — pushing leased public land toward actual production.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding undeveloped federal leases, who would face civil penalties, stricter development benchmarks, shortened lease terms, and doubled renewal rents if they failed to produce.

drawbacks.text: The bill would not have directly lowered prices: idled leases are often idle because they are uneconomic to drill, and forcing development could add little near-term supply while adding compliance costs and civil penalties for companies holding acreage.

It would have tightened lease terms for all operators, including those developing diligently, by limiting renewals to one-year periods at double the rental rate unless active production or good-faith progress is shown.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — forcing companies to use public oil and gas leases they already hold, or give them back — was real but modest: it would not itself add much production, since companies idle leases mainly because drilling is uneconomic there, and it imposed new rules and doubled renewal rents on legitimate operators too. The defeat's cost was leaving the "use it or lose it" pressure in place only as rhetoric. As policy, it was a sound but narrow push; as politics in a $4-a-gallon summer, it was drawn partly to force a vote Republicans would have to defend.

outcome.mechanism: The House voted on it under a fast-track rule needing a two-thirds majority; it got 223 votes to 195, short of the 290 or so needed, and died there.

narrative.text: The House voted on June 26, 2008, under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority and no amendments.
It failed 223-195, with 212 of 235 Democrats voting yes and only 11 of 199 Republicans doing so.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill never reached the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding undeveloped federal oil and gas leases kept them without new use-it-or-lose-it conditions, and the status quo on public-land leasing continued.

for.name: Nick J. Rahall II
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and moved to suspend the rules and pass it on the House floor.

for.name: 212 of 235 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the motion to pass the bill.

against.name: 176 of 199 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split sharply by party: 212 of 235 Democrats voted yes while only 11 of 199 Republicans did.

industries.note: Companies sitting on undeveloped federal leases would have to develop them or give them up, face civil penalties, and pay doubled rents on one-year lease renewals.
Operators actively drilling would keep access to new leases but face tighter renewal terms and higher rents; the burden falls hardest on companies speculating in undeveloped acreage.
Land locked up in idle leases returns to competitive leasing, with the public collecting rents and royalties on acreage actually producing.
